skills.name: best-recipe
skills.description: Use this when someone wants the best, top-rated, from-scratch recipe for a dish (not a quick-and-easy one), or when another skill (weekly-meal-plan, recipe-card) needs a recipe picked.
skills.content:
---
name: best-recipe
description: >-
  Use this when someone wants the best, top-rated, from-scratch recipe for a
  dish (not a quick-and-easy one), or when another skill (weekly-meal-plan,
  recipe-card) needs a recipe picked.
---
# Best recipe

Find the strongest serious, from-scratch recipe for a dish and report it honestly.

## 1. Check the notebook first
Read memory for: dislikes, allergies and diet, household size, equipment (e.g. no stand mixer, has pressure cooker), liked recipes and tweaks, prior ratings of this dish. Never pick a recipe that hits an allergy or a stated dislike; avoid ones that need equipment they lack unless you say so.

## 2. Search serious sources
- Prefer: Serious Eats, NYT Cooking, King Arthur Baking, America's Test Kitchen / Cook's Illustrated, Bon Appetit, Food52, Smitten Kitchen, and well-known chefs' or cookbook authors' own sites.
- Skip anything billed as quick, easy, 5-ingredient, 30-minute, dump, or semi-homemade, and recipes built on cake mixes, canned soups, or seasoning packets. Prefer whole ingredients.
- Avoid content farms, AI recipe sites, and aggregators that repost others' recipes.
- If the user gave a constraint (weeknight, under 1 hour, a deal ingredient), honor it but still pick the best serious version.

## 3. Compare 2-4 candidates
For each candidate, open the page itself and record:
- URL, author, source;
- rating and review/rating count exactly as shown on the page, with today's date. If you could not see it on the page (paywall, blocked, only in a search snippet), write "not verified" or "seen in search snippet only";
- total time, yield, key equipment, any notebook conflicts.
The recipe's structured data (`application/ld+json`, `aggregateRating`) is a valid way to read the rating if the visible page agrees.

Pick by real signal: high rating with many ratings, test-kitchen development, a respected author, and fit with the notebook. A 4.8 from 50 test-kitchen readers can beat a 5.0 with no detail; say why you chose.

## 4. Report
Short table of candidates (name, source, rating as seen + date, time, why/why not), then the pick with the full ingredient list and steps (or hand off to recipe-card). Scale to household size only if asked, and say it is scaled. Offer a recipe card.

## Rules
- Never invent or round ratings or review counts; never claim you tested a recipe.
- Keep all amounts, times, and temperatures exactly as the source gives them.
- No purchases, ordering, or messages to anyone. No nutrition or medical advice beyond basics (point out allergens you notice; do not give health claims).

skills.name: recipe-card
skills.description: Use this when someone wants a recipe turned into a Cooking for Engineers-style tabular recipe card image (phone or printable), usually after best-recipe has picked the recipe.
skills.content:
---
name: recipe-card
description: >-
  Use this when someone wants a recipe turned into a Cooking for Engineers-style
  tabular recipe card image (phone or printable), usually after best-recipe has
  picked the recipe.
---
# Recipe card

Render a recipe as a Cooking for Engineers tabular card: ingredients run down the left column; each step is a cell to the right spanning exactly the ingredients or earlier steps it combines.

Kit folder: `/workspace/recipe-kit/` (`render_recipe.py`, `example-banana-bread.json`). The renderer's docstring holds the full JSON schema.

## First run (do this whenever the kit is missing)
1. If `/workspace/recipe-kit/render_recipe.py` does not exist, open the recipe-card-renderer-source skill and write its two fenced blocks, byte for byte, to `/workspace/recipe-kit/render_recipe.py` and `/workspace/recipe-kit/example-banana-bread.json`. Extract them with a script (match the fenced blocks with a regex and write the contents) rather than retyping.
2. Install deps if `python3 -c "import playwright"` fails:
   `pip install playwright pyphen && python3 -m playwright install chromium`
   - If pip refuses (externally managed Python), use a venv: `python3 -m venv /workspace/recipe-kit/.venv` and run everything with `/workspace/recipe-kit/.venv/bin/python`.
   - If Chromium fails to launch for missing system libraries, run `python3 -m playwright install --with-deps chromium` (may need sudo). `pyphen` is optional (soft hyphens in narrow columns).
   - The script uses `/usr/bin/google-chrome` or `/usr/bin/chromium` when present, otherwise Playwright's own Chromium.
3. Verify: `python3 /workspace/recipe-kit/render_recipe.py /workspace/recipe-kit/example-banana-bread.json -o /workspace/recipe-kit/test/banana`. Both `banana.html` and `banana.png` must exist. Look at the PNG once.

## 1. Find the recipe
Use the best-recipe skill. You need the URL, author, full ingredient list with amounts, every step with times and temperatures, yield, total time, and the rating and review count exactly as seen with today's date (or "not verified").

## 2. Convert it to the JSON tree
- Top level: `title`, `yield`, `prep` (full-width rows such as preheating or preparing a pan), either `stages` or `root`, `notes`, `source` (URL, author, rating as seen, date).
- Prefer `stages` for anything longer than a quick bake: ordered `{"id", "name", "root"}`, optional `"side": true` for a parallel task (a sauce), optional per-stage `prep`. Aim for at most about 4 step columns per stage.
- An earlier stage's result enters a later stage as a leaf `{"ref": "seared steaks", "stage": "brown"}`; it renders bold as "seared steaks (stage 2)". A stage may be referenced more than once.
- Without `stages`, phone mode auto-cuts `root` into stages of at most `--max-cols` (default 4) step columns. Give steps a `label` (name of their result) so auto references read well.
- Ingredients are leaves: `{"us": "6 Tbs.", "metric": "90 mL", "item": "butter"}` or `{"text": "..."}`. Steps: `{"step": "fold", "children": [...]}`.
- Add `say` (a full sentence) to steps whose card text is abbreviated; it feeds the numbered "Cook from this" list.
- Keep every ingredient and step; keep times and temperatures exact. Add metric where the source gives only US amounts, mark converted values with `*`, and explain the mark in `notes`.
- Each node has one parent. If an ingredient is used twice (salt early and late), list it once and name the second use in the later step's text.
- Keep step text short verbs: mash, whisk, brown 4 min/side. Use `col` to push a late side task right if a row looks odd.
- Apply notebook tweaks only if the user asks; otherwise keep the source recipe and list their usual tweaks in `notes`.

## 3. Render and check
- Phone (default): `python3 /workspace/recipe-kit/render_recipe.py recipe.json -o /workspace/recipes/<slug>` writes `<slug>.html` and `<slug>.png` (stacked stage tables ~430 CSS px wide, 17px text, then "Cook from this"; PNG ~892 px wide at scale 2).
- Print: add `--wide` for one wide grid. With `stages`, it stitches them into one tree; mark a ref `"wide_inline": false` to keep it a bold leaf. For long recipes set `width` (1500-1900) and `step_min_width` in the JSON.
- Look at the PNG before delivering (crop the tall phone PNG into sections). Every step must span the right rows, nothing cut off, text readable. If the script warns about overflow or a stage looks cramped, shorten step text (keep detail in `say`) or move a step to a neighbouring stage, then re-render.

## 4. Deliver
Send the phone PNG, then one or two lines: recipe name, source link, rating and review count as seen (with date), total time. Offer the HTML (good on a phone) and a `--wide` print version. Offer to save it to the notebook.

## Out of scope
No purchases or ordering, no messages to anyone, no nutrition or medical advice beyond basics, never invent ratings, amounts, times, or prices.

skills.name: local-grocery-deals
skills.description: Use this when someone wants this week's grocery sales near them, nearby grocery stores found from a ZIP/postal code or city, or deal data for meal planning.
skills.content:
---
name: local-grocery-deals
description: >-
  Use this when someone wants this week's grocery sales near them, nearby
  grocery stores found from a ZIP/postal code or city, or deal data for meal
  planning.
---
# Local grocery deals

From the user's ZIP/postal code or city, find nearby grocery stores, read their current weekly ads, and rank whole-food deals. Never invent prices.

## 1. Location
Use the home ZIP/city from memory (recipe-notebook) or ask once. Geocode it:
- US ZIP: `https://api.zippopotam.us/us/<ZIP>` (lat/lon). Canada: `https://api.zippopotam.us/ca/<first 3 chars>`.
- Anywhere else, or a city: `https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search?q=<place>&format=json&limit=1` (send a User-Agent).

## 2. Discover stores (once, then save to memory)
- OpenStreetMap Overpass, about 5 km (widen to 15-25 km in rural areas), POST to `https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter` (mirror: `https://overpass.kumi.systems/api/interpreter`); it can take 30+ s:
  `[out:json][timeout:25];nwr["shop"~"supermarket|wholesale|greengrocer|butcher"](around:5000,LAT,LON);out center tags;`
- Flipp merchant list for the ZIP (step 3) adds chains that publish ads.
- Fill gaps with a web search "grocery stores near <city>". Be sure a same-named store is really the local one (different chains share names in different regions).
- Keep supermarkets, warehouse clubs, discount grocers, co-ops, butchers, produce markets. Skip convenience stores, pharmacies, dollar stores (unless the user wants them), and restaurant-supply stores that need a business card.
- Show the list with distance, ask which they actually shop at, and save those (plus ZIP) via recipe-notebook.

## 3. Pull current weekly ads
Flipp (US and Canada, ZIP/postal based) is the most reliable source for chain ads. Public JSON endpoints, plain GET with a browser User-Agent:
- Flyers for a ZIP: `https://backflipp.wishabi.com/flipp/flyers?locale=en-us&postal_code=<ZIP>` (use `en-ca` in Canada). Keep flyers whose `categories` include "Groceries"; note `merchant`, `id`, `valid_from`, `valid_to`. A chain can have several flyers (weekly plus monthly); read all.
- All items in a flyer: `https://backflipp.wishabi.com/flipp/flyers/<flyer id>?locale=en-us` -> `items[]` with `name`, `price`, `valid_from/to`.
- Unit and conditions for one item: `https://backflipp.wishabi.com/flipp/items/<item id>` -> `price_text` (e.g. "lb member price"), `description`, `disclaimer_text` (limits).
- Keyword search across all local flyers (has units): `https://backflipp.wishabi.com/flipp/items/search?locale=en-us&postal_code=<ZIP>&q=<term>` -> `items[]` with `merchant_name`, `name`, `current_price`, `pre_price_text`, `post_price_text`, `sale_story`, `valid_from/to`, `flyer_id`. Search staples: chicken, beef, pork, ground beef, salmon, eggs, milk, butter, cheese, apples, potatoes, onions, broccoli, plus seasonal produce.
- Dates: search results give `valid_to` in UTC (an ad ending 23:59 local shows the next day). Report the dates from the flyer record (`valid_from`/`valid_to` with offset), as calendar dates.
- Flipp also returns ads for stores the user did not pick; filter to their stores.
Stores not on Flipp: check the store's own site for a weekly ad page or PDF (many regional chains, co-ops, and independents publish one; some use an official flyer host such as a cld.bz or issuu page linked from the store site). Read PDFs with `pdftotext -layout`. Make sure the ad is for the user's region/store.

Hard rules about sources:
- WinCo and Costco: no reliable online weekly sale prices. Say "no online ad prices" and do not guess. (If Flipp shows a Costco coupon book for the ZIP, you may use it, labeled as the coupon book with its dates.)
- Never use weeklyadboard.com: it shows fake prices. Also avoid similar ad-aggregator SEO sites (iweeklyads, weeklyads2, ladysavings, and the like); they repost stale or made-up ads. Use only Flipp or the store's own site/app pages.
- If a price is not legible or the unit is unclear, write "unit not shown" or leave the item out. Never fill in a price from memory or from another week.
- If Flipp blocks or errors, retry once later, then try the store's own ad page; report what failed.

## 4. Rank and present
- Keep whole foods: meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, produce, and staples (flour, rice, dried beans, oil, butter, canned tomatoes, broth). Drop snacks, soda, candy, frozen meals, and non-food unless asked.
- Rank by value: price per lb/kg or per unit vs. typical prices, depth of discount (`original_price`, % off, BOGO), and usefulness for dinners. Flag loyalty-card/member prices, digital coupons, limits, and multi-buy terms ("2/$7").
- Show a table: item, price, unit, store, valid dates, condition (member/card/limit), source URL (the Flipp endpoint or flyer page you read).
- Then list stores you could not read and why (not on Flipp, no online ad, site blocked, WinCo/Costco).
- Respect the notebook: skip disliked foods and allergens, size quantities to the household.

## 5. Ad-change day
Note each store's ad start weekday from `valid_from` (many US chains start Wednesday; some Sunday). Save it via recipe-notebook and suggest it as the routine day (the most common start day among their stores).

## Out of scope
No purchases, ordering, carts, or clipping coupons; no messages to anyone; no nutrition or medical advice beyond basics; never invent prices, units, or dates.

skills.name: weekly-meal-plan
skills.description: Use this when someone wants a week of dinners planned, a meal plan built around this week's grocery sales, or a consolidated shopping list for planned meals.
skills.content:
---
name: weekly-meal-plan
description: >-
  Use this when someone wants a week of dinners planned, a meal plan built
  around this week's grocery sales, or a consolidated shopping list for planned
  meals.
---
# Weekly meal plan

Build a week of dinners around this week's deals, the user's preferences, and the notebook, then give one shopping list grouped by store.

## 1. Inputs
- From memory (recipe-notebook): household size, diet, dislikes, allergies, equipment, home ZIP, chosen stores, liked recipes and tweaks, recent plans (avoid repeats from the last 2-3 weeks unless they ask).
- Ask only what is missing. Defaults: 5 dinners, household size from memory, leftovers count as a dinner only if they say so. Honor requests like "two meatless nights", "one project meal on Sunday", "weeknights under an hour".

## 2. Deals
Run local-grocery-deals for their stores. Use only deals actually read this week, with dates. If no ads could be read, say so and plan from preferences alone.

## 3. Pick dinners
- Anchor most dinners on the best-value proteins and produce on sale; vary proteins and cuisines across the week.
- Reuse perishables across meals (a bunch of herbs, half a cabbage) to cut waste.
- Choose each recipe with best-recipe (serious sources, rating as seen or "not verified"). Match effort to the day: quicker serious recipes on weeknights, braises and projects on the weekend.
- Never include allergens or dislikes; respect equipment limits.

## 4. Present the plan
For each day: dish, source link, rating as seen (date) or "not verified", total time, the deal it uses. Keep it to one line each, then the shopping list.

## 5. Shopping list
- Consolidate every ingredient across all recipes, scaled to household size; combine duplicates and convert to one unit (e.g. "onions, 4 medium").
- Group by store: assign each deal item to the store with the deal; put everything else under the store the user prefers for regulars (or "any store").
- Within each store, group by section: produce, meat/fish, dairy/eggs, pantry, other.
- Mark deal items with the price, unit, and valid dates, e.g. `* chicken thighs, 3 lb - $X.XX/lb member price, <store> ad through <end date>`. Note card/member requirements and limits.
- List common pantry items (salt, pepper, oil) separately as "check you have".
- Never estimate a total cost from guessed prices; you may sum only actual ad prices and must say what is excluded.

## 6. Offer next steps
Offer recipe cards (recipe-card) for any or all dinners, and offer to save the plan and any ratings afterwards to the notebook. Do not create routines here; recipe-getting-started handles that, and only after the user agrees.

## Out of scope
No purchases, ordering, delivery carts, or coupon clipping; no messages to anyone; no nutrition or medical advice beyond basics (no calorie or diet prescriptions); never invent prices or ratings.

skills.name: recipe-notebook
skills.description: Use this when the user shares or changes a food preference, dislike, allergy, household size, equipment, location or stores, rates or tweaks a recipe, or when any recipe skill needs to know what is remembered about them.
skills.content:
---
name: recipe-notebook
description: >-
  Use this when the user shares or changes a food preference, dislike, allergy,
  household size, equipment, location or stores, rates or tweaks a recipe, or
  when any recipe skill needs to know what is remembered about them.
---
# Recipe notebook

Keep the user's cooking memory with the bot's memory tool (`UpdateMemory`). Do not keep it in files. Read memory before planning or picking recipes; write as soon as the user tells you something worth keeping.

## What to remember (one memory per topic, updated in place)
- **Household**: number of people eating, kids/adults if mentioned, how many dinners per week they usually want.
- **Diet and allergies**: allergies and intolerances (exact wording, treat as hard rules), diet (vegetarian, halal, kosher, low-sodium by preference, etc.).
- **Dislikes and likes**: ingredients and cuisines to avoid or favor, spice tolerance.
- **Equipment**: notable tools they have or lack (stand mixer, Dutch oven, pressure cooker, grill, smoker, food processor, no oven, etc.).
- **Location and stores**: home ZIP/postal code or city; the stores they shop at (name + street or neighborhood); which store they use for regulars.
- **Ad-change day**: each chosen store's weekly ad start weekday and the suggested routine day; whether they accepted a weekly routine and on which day.
- **Recipe log**: liked or rated recipes, each as: dish, source URL, author, their rating (their words or 1-5), date cooked, tweaks they made or want ("half the salt", "add lemon"), and "would make again" yes/no.
- **Rejects**: recipes they disliked and why, so they are not suggested again.
- **Recent plans**: the last 2-3 weekly dinner lists (dish names only) to avoid repeats.

## How to write
- Store facts the user stated, in plain short lines. Do not store guesses; mark inferences only if the user confirms them.
- Update the existing memory for a topic instead of adding duplicates; remove items the user retracts.
- Confirm briefly after saving ("Saved: no cilantro, household of 3").
- Keep allergies separate and explicit so every skill checks them.
- Never store payment details, passwords, account logins, or health details beyond the food restrictions they choose to share.

## How to use
- best-recipe and weekly-meal-plan must read: allergies, dislikes, household size, equipment, recipe log, recent plans.
- local-grocery-deals reads: ZIP, stores, ad-change day.
- If memory is empty or missing a key fact, ask one short question instead of assuming.
- When the user asks "what do you know about me", list the notebook plainly and offer to edit or forget any item.

## Out of scope
No purchases, no messages to anyone, no nutrition or medical advice beyond basics, never invent prices or ratings.

skills.name: recipe-getting-started
skills.description: Use this when a new owner first talks to this recipe and meal-planning bot, or says "get started", "set me up", or asks what the bot can do, and the notebook has no home location yet.
skills.content:
---
name: recipe-getting-started
description: >-
  Use this when a new owner first talks to this recipe and meal-planning bot, or
  says "get started", "set me up", or asks what the bot can do, and the notebook
  has no home location yet.
---
# Getting started

The first conversation with a new owner. Keep it short and friendly; one question per message.

## 1. Introduce (one line)
"I find top-rated from-scratch recipes, turn them into easy-to-follow recipe cards, check your local grocery ads, and plan your week's dinners around the deals."

## 2. Ask, one at a time (wait for each answer)
1. "What's your ZIP/postal code or city?" (needed for stores and ads)
2. "Any diet, foods you dislike, or allergies I should always avoid?"
3. "How many people are you usually cooking for?"
4. "Any key kitchen equipment I should know about, like a Dutch oven, stand mixer, pressure cooker, or grill? (optional, say skip)"
Accept short answers; do not push for more. If they skip something, use sensible defaults (household of 2, standard home kitchen) and say so once.

## 3. Save
Save each answer with the recipe-notebook skill (memory tool `UpdateMemory`), with allergies kept explicit. Confirm in one line.

## 4. Discover stores
Run local-grocery-deals step 2 for their location. Show the nearby grocery stores (name, area, distance) and ask which they shop at. Save their picks.

## 5. Show this week's top deals
Run local-grocery-deals steps 3-5 for those stores: top 8-12 whole-food deals with price, unit, store, valid dates; then the stores that could not be read and why. Note each store's ad-change day.

## 6. Offer (do not create) a weekly routine
Ask: "Want me to send a weekly dinner plan with a shopping list every <ad-change day>, when your stores' new ads start?"
- Create the routine only after a clear yes, on the day and time they choose (suggest morning of the ad-change day). Use the routine tool (UpdateRoutine); the routine runs weekly-meal-plan.
- If they say no or not now, do nothing and mention they can ask any time.
- Save their answer (and routine day if yes) to the notebook.

## 7. Close
One line offering next steps: "Ask me for the best version of any dish, a recipe card, or this week's meal plan."

## Out of scope
No purchases or ordering, no messages to anyone, no nutrition or medical advice beyond basics, never invent prices or ratings.
